stages.title: Language sounds and pronunciation
stages.hook: Say "a, i, u, e, o" slowly. Japanese has five clean vowels, and each sound takes the same beat.
explain: Japanese has five vowels: あ (a), い (i), う (u), え (e), お (o). They are short and clear, like Spanish vowels. Japanese is said in beats called morae. Each kana is one beat: さかな (sa-ka-na) has three beats.

A long vowel takes two beats and can change a word. おばさん (obasan, aunt) and おばあさん (obāsan, grandmother) are different words. In romaji, a line over the vowel (ā, ī, ū, ē, ō) shows the long vowel. Japanese also has pitch accent: the pitch of the voice goes high and low, and, for example, あめ can mean rain or candy depending on the pitch.
stages.mnemonic: Five vowels, one beat each: a-i-u-e-o.

gq.q: How many beats are in さかな?
o: Two, because of the two syllables ka and na
Four, because of the long vowel
Six, counting each letter in romaji
gq.why: Each kana is one beat, so さ-か-な has three.

gq.q: What difference do おばさん and おばあさん show?
o: Nothing, they are the same word spelled twice
Only the spelling, not the sound
Only the tone of the voice, not the length
gq.why: A long vowel is longer and changes the meaning.

panel.q: Why is vowel length important in Japanese?
o: It does not matter, since listeners guess
It marks a question at the end of a sentence
It marks a plural, like -s in English
panel.why: A long vowel adds a beat, so the length can distinguish words.

panel.q: The word あめ can mean rain or candy. What helps tell them apart?
panel.why: Pitch accent and context separate them.

panel.q: A learner says どうも as "dō-mo" with the first vowel short. What might happen?
o: Nothing at all will change in meaning or sound
It will become a question by mistake
It will turn into a katakana word automatically
panel.why: Shortening a long vowel can make the word sound different.

teach.model: Japanese has five vowels: a, i, u, e, o. Each kana is one beat. A long vowel takes two beats and can change the word, for example obasan and obāsan.

points.ask: How many vowels does Japanese have?
How long does each kana take?
What does a long vowel do?

trip.prompt: Listen to the five vowels in a sample and say them aloud.

stages.title: Alphabet, script or basic characters
stages.hook: Japanese uses three kinds of writing in one sentence. Can you spot them?
explain: Japanese uses hiragana (ひらがな), katakana (カタカナ) and kanji (漢字) together. Hiragana is used for native words and grammar endings. Katakana is used for foreign words (like コーヒー, coffee), names and emphasis. Kanji are characters from China that carry meaning, like 山 (mountain) and 川 (river).

Each kana stands for a sound: あ is a, か is ka. There are 46 basic hiragana and 46 basic katakana. Kanji have usually two kinds of readings: a Japanese reading (kun) and a Chinese-derived reading (on). 山 is やま (yama) alone and さん (-san) in words such as 富士山 (Fujisan).

Rōmaji is the Latin-letter spelling of Japanese. This course uses Hepburn romaji, which shows the sounds, like shi, chi and tsu. Writing runs left to right in horizontal text, and in some books, from top to bottom and right to left.
stages.mnemonic: Hiragana is soft and round, katakana is sharp for foreign words.

gq.q: Which script is used for foreign words like コーヒー?
What does the character 山 mean?
o: River, because of the flowing lines
Sea, as in the word for ocean
Rain, as in the character 雨

panel.q: Why does 山 have two readings, やま and さん?
panel.why: Kanji have Japanese (kun) and Chinese-derived (on) readings.

panel.q: A shop sign has "ラーメン". Which script is it?
panel.why: ラーメン is written in katakana for a loanword (from Chinese).

panel.q: Which statement about kanji is correct?
o: They are only sounds, like hiragana and katakana, with no meaning
They carry meaning and came from Chinese characters
They are only used for foreign words and names, like katakana
They are the Latin alphabet used for writing Japanese
panel.why: Kanji are Chinese-derived characters that carry meaning.

teach.model: Japanese uses hiragana for native words and endings, katakana for foreign words and names, and kanji for meaning. Romaji spells Japanese with Latin letters.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of a Japanese sign and name each script you see.

stages.title: Greetings and introductions
stages.hook: In Japan, people bow when they meet. What do they say when they greet each other?
explain: Greetings depend on the time of day. おはよう (ohayō) is good morning, and the polite form is おはようございます. こんにちは (konnichiwa) is hello in the daytime, and こんばんは (konbanwa) is good evening. さようなら (sayōnara) is goodbye.

To thank, say ありがとう (arigatō), and politely ありがとうございます. The reply is どういたしまして (dō itashimashite). すみません (sumimasen) means excuse me or sorry. When you meet someone for the first time, say はじめまして (hajimemashite) and then よろしくおねがいします.

To say your name, use わたしは…です (I am…). The ending です (desu) is polite. In Japan, the family name comes first, and people often add さん (-san) to someone else's name, but never to their own. Bowing is common and shows respect.
stages.mnemonic: Say hajimemashite, then your name, then yoroshiku.
sentences: Nice to meet you, please treat me well.

gq.q: Which is said when meeting someone for the first time?
o: ありがとうございます
gq.why: はじめまして is used at a first meeting.

gq.q: Which word is a reply to ありがとう?
gq.why: どういたしまして means you are welcome.

panel.q: A person says "I am Tanaka-san". What is wrong?
o: You do not add -san to your own name
Nothing is wrong, because -san is always polite
Tanaka is not a real name, so it cannot be used
-san is a verb, so it must come at the end
panel.why: Japanese people do not add -san to their own name.

panel.q: At 8 pm, which greeting is right?
panel.why: こんばんは is the evening greeting.

panel.q: Why does the family name come first in Japan?
o: It is a spelling rule of hiragana writing
It is a mistake that foreigners made long ago
It is the Japanese naming order
Because the given name is written in katakana
panel.why: Japanese naming order puts the family name before the given name.

teach.model: Japanese greetings change with the time of day: ohayō, konnichiwa, konbanwa. At a first meeting say hajimemashite. Use -san after other people's names but not your own.

points.ask: What do I say at a first meeting?

trip.prompt: Read about -san and note when it is not used.

stages.title: Numbers and counting
stages.hook: How many fingers do you have? In Japanese, the number words are short and regular.
explain: The Chinese-derived numbers are 一 ichi, 二 ni, 三 san, 四 yon or shi, 五 go, 六 roku, 七 nana or shichi, 八 hachi, 九 kyū, 十 jū. Bigger numbers are built by combining: 十一 is jūichi (11), 二十 is nijū (20). Four and seven have two readings, and yon and nana are more common today.

Japanese also has native counting words for small numbers of things: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ. To count people, use ひとり (one person), ふたり (two people) and then さんにん, よにん. Age is counted with the counter 歳 (sai): 五歳 (gosai) is five years old.

The number four, shi, sounds like the word for death, so people often prefer yon. Hospitals and apartments may avoid the number four in some places. Counting words (counters) change depending on the shape and kind of object.
stages.mnemonic: Use yon and nana for four and seven in daily speech.

gq.why: 十 and 一 are combined as jūichi.

gq.q: Why do many people say yon instead of shi for four?
gq.why: Shi sounds like the word for death, so yon is preferred.

panel.q: What is 二十 read as?
panel.why: 二 is ni and 十 is jū, so nijū.

panel.q: A child counts two people. Which word is correct?
panel.why: Two people is ふたり.

panel.q: Why are there different counting words in Japanese?
o: They are random and must be guessed each time
They are only used to show the tones of numbers
They are only needed when writing in kanji
Counters depend on the kind of object
panel.why: Counters change with the type or shape of the thing counted.

teach.model: The numbers are ichi, ni, san, yon, go, roku, nana, hachi, kyū, jū. Bigger numbers are combined, so 11 is jūichi. People are counted with hitori, futari, and so on.

points.ask: How do I make bigger numbers?

trip.prompt: Find the numbers 1 to 10 and note which have two readings.

stages.title: Colours and shapes
stages.hook: What colour is the sky? What shape is the moon? Japanese colours often end in い.
explain: Some colours are adjectives that end in い (i): あかい (red), あおい (blue), しろい (white) and くろい (black). The noun forms are あか, あお, しろ and くろ. Others are only nouns: きいろ (yellow) and みどり (green). 黄色い (kiiroi) also works as an adjective.
Say りんごはあかいです (apples are red). To describe a noun, put the adjective before it: あかいりんご (a red apple). For shapes, まる (circle) and しかく (square) are common words, and まるい is the adjective round.
In Japanese, あお covers both blue and, in some phrases, green: traffic lights go "ao" for green, and 青りんご means green apple. This shows that colour words do not always match across languages.
stages.mnemonic: Four basic colours take い: あかい, あおい, しろい, くろい.

gq.q: How do you say "a red apple"?
gq.why: The adjective comes before the noun.

panel.q: In Japan, what colour is a traffic light "go" signal called?
panel.why: It is commonly called あお (blue), though it looks green.

panel.q: What does this show about colour words?
o: All languages share exactly the same colour words
Colours have no names in Japanese until modern times
Colour words are always nouns in every language
panel.why: Colour categories differ across languages.

panel.q: Which is not an い-adjective colour?
panel.why: みどり is a noun and not an い-adjective.

teach.model: Colours like aka, ao, shiro and kuro can be adjectives with い. Kiiro and midori are mostly nouns. The adjective goes before the noun, as in akai ringo.

trip.prompt: Read about ao and midori and note what is special about them.

stages.title: Family and people
stages.hook: In Japanese, you call your own mum one thing and someone else's mum another. Why?
explain: Family words change for your own family and other people's family. Others' mother is おかあさん (okāsan) and your own mother is はは (haha). Others' father is おとうさん (otōsan) and your own is ちち (chichi). In a family, children use おかあさん to their own mother, too.
Siblings show age. おにいさん (onīsan) is an older brother and おねえさん (onēsan) is an older sister. Younger siblings are おとうと (otōto) and いもうと (imōto). Grandparents are おじいさん (ojīsan) and おばあさん (obāsan).

The use of "uchi" (inside) and "soto" (outside) groups is an important idea. When talking to outsiders, you lower your own group and honour the other's. That is why one word for a mum changes with the speaker and listener.
stages.mnemonic: Inside the family: haha, chichi. Outside: okāsan, otōsan.

gq.why: いもうと is a younger sister.

gq.q: How would you talk to a friend about your own mother?
gq.why: To outsiders you use はは for your own mother.

panel.q: Why is "obāsan" different from "obasan"?
o: They are the same word, written two ways
One is used only by men and one by women
One is a place name and the other is a person
panel.why: The long ā makes it grandmother, and the short a makes it aunt.

panel.q: What does the uchi–soto idea explain?
o: Different words for own and others' family
The rules for counting the people in a family
The order of the kanji in family names
The pitch accent of words for relatives
panel.why: It explains why words differ for your own group and other people's group.

panel.q: A child calls to their mother in the kitchen. Which word is natural?
panel.why: Children call their own mother おかあさん directly.

teach.model: Japanese has different words for your own family and other people's family: haha and okāsan. Siblings show age, and long vowels matter, as in obāsan and obasan.

trip.prompt: Read about uchi-soto and note one example.

stages.title: Common objects
stages.hook: Look around you. Which things are near you, and which are far? Japanese has special words for that.
explain: Japanese has three pointing words: これ (kore) is this, near me; それ (sore) is that, near you; and あれ (are) is that over there, far from both. Say これはほんです (this is a book). The particle は marks the topic and です is the polite ending.
Common objects: ほん (book), つくえ (desk), いす (chair), かばん (bag), えんぴつ (pencil), とけい (clock or watch), かさ (umbrella) and ぼうし (hat). The particle の shows belonging: わたしのほん (my book).
To say where something is, use に and あります for things: つくえのうえにかばんがあります (there is a bag on the desk). For living things, use います. Japanese does not use "a" or "the".
stages.mnemonic: Kore near me, sore near you, are far from both.
sentences: There is a bag on the desk.
That over there is a clock.

gq.why: あれ points to something far from both people.

gq.q: Which particle shows "my" in わたしのほん?

panel.q: Which verb is used for a bag on the desk?
panel.why: あります is for things that do not move on their own.

panel.q: Your friend holds a pen. What do you say?
o: これは ペンですか
それは ペンですか
あれは ペンですか
ここは ペンですか
panel.why: それ points to something near the listener.

panel.q: Why does Japanese not need "a" or "the"?
panel.why: Japanese has no articles.

teach.model: Kore means this one near me, sore means that one near you and are means that one far away. の shows belonging, and に あります tells where something is.

points.ask: What are the three pointing words?
How do I say where something is?

trip.prompt: Find kosoado words and place them on a diagram.

stages.title: Everyday actions
stages.hook: Can you act out eating, drinking and running? Japanese verbs end with -masu when polite.
explain: Dictionary-form verbs end in -u: たべる (eat), のむ (drink), みる (see), きく (listen), はなす (speak), あるく (walk), はしる (run), ねる (sleep). The polite form ends in -masu: たべます, のみます, みます. The verb comes at the end of the sentence.
Particles mark roles. を marks the thing acted on: ごはんをたべます (I eat rice). で marks where an action happens: こうえんではしります (I run in the park). が marks the subject, especially in descriptions: いぬがはしります.
Negative polite forms use -masen: たべません (do not eat). Japanese verbs do not change for person or number, so たべます can mean I eat, you eat or he eats. Context tells who.
stages.mnemonic: Verb last: object を, place で, verb ます.
sentences: The dog runs in the park.

gq.q: Where does the verb go in a Japanese sentence?
gq.why: The verb comes at the end.

gq.q: Which particle marks the object of an action?
gq.why: を marks the thing acted on.

panel.q: How do you say "I do not eat" politely?
o: たべない です only
panel.why: -masen is the negative polite ending.

panel.q: Which particle marks where the action takes place?
panel.why: で marks the place of an action.

panel.q: Why can たべます mean I eat, you eat or she eats?
o: It is a mistake, and only one meaning is correct
Each pronoun is built into the verb ending
Only the tone of voice tells who is acting
Verbs do not change for person
panel.why: Japanese verbs do not change for person.

teach.model: The verb goes last. Particles mark the roles: を for the object, で for the place. The polite form ends in masu, and masen is the negative.

trip.prompt: Find the table of masu forms and read three.

stages.title: Simple listening and speaking
stages.hook: If someone speaks too fast in Japanese, what can you say? Polite requests are your best friend.
explain: Helpful phrases keep a conversation alive. はい (hai) is yes and いいえ (iie) is no. わかりました (wakarimashita) means I understood, and わかりません (wakarimasen) means I do not understand. もういちどおねがいします (mō ichido onegaishimasu) means please say it once more.

To ask someone to speak slowly, say ゆっくりおねがいします or ゆっくりはなしてください. ください (kudasai) with a verb ending in -te makes a polite request. Because "hai" can also mean "I am listening", it does not always mean agreement.

Listen for the sentence ending, because the verb and the polite ending come last. Repeat what you hear, and use short answers. Nodding and the small sound あいづち (aizuchi), such as はい or ええ, show that you are following.
stages.mnemonic: Slow, again, please: yukkuri, mō ichido, onegaishimasu.
items: もう一度 お願いします
ゆっくり お願いします

gq.q: What does わかりません mean?
gq.why: わかりません is the negative of understand.

gq.q: Which request asks a speaker to slow down?
o: もう いちど いって ください
ゆっくり はなして ください
わかりました、ありがとう

panel.q: In conversation, a listener keeps saying はい. What might it mean?
panel.why: はい can signal that you are listening, not necessarily agreeing.

panel.q: What is あいづち?
o: A kind of kanji used in old letters
A pitch accent rule for short words
A greeting used when people meet
panel.why: Aizuchi are short responses showing you are following the speaker.

panel.q: Why listen for the end of the sentence?
o: The verb comes at the end
The subject comes last in Japanese
The end of a sentence is always silent
The end of a sentence is optional
panel.why: The verb and polite ending come last.

teach.model: If I do not understand, I can say wakarimasen and ask for the speaker to repeat or speak slowly. Adding onegaishimasu or kudasai makes it polite. Hai can show that I am listening.

points.ask: What do I say if I do not understand?
What can I ask the speaker?

trip.prompt: Read about aizuchi and list two examples.
